cues.text: Section eight: Change management, technology and people.
Change management has two related meanings.
The first is technical change control, which manages modifications to systems safely.
The second is organisational change management, which helps individuals and teams adopt new processes, technologies and behaviours.
Both are required for successful transformation.

A system can be changed flawlessly from a technical point of view and still fail if people do not adopt it, and the reverse is also true: enthusiastic users cannot rescue a change that breaks the service.
Now consider what drives change.
The drivers include new technology, regulatory obligations, competition, customer expectations, mergers, cloud migration and security threats.
To make this concrete, think of a hospital replacing paper records with an electronic system.
That hospital must manage deployment risk, so that the new system works safely and reliably.
It must also help clinicians adopt new workflows, so that the people who rely on the system can actually use it in their daily work.
Notice that this single example contains both meanings of change management: the technical side and the human side.
Next, the types of technical change.
A technical change may be standard, which means it is routine and pre-authorised.
It may be normal, which means it is assessed and authorised according to its risk.
Or it may be an emergency change, which is expedited because of urgency.
An important qualification applies here: emergency does not mean uncontrolled.
Even when speed matters most, the change still needs appropriate control and accountability.
Then we come to the change lifecycle.
It includes planning and risk assessment, approval, implementation, monitoring and review.

Within this lifecycle, a request for change records several things: the purpose, the scope, the affected services, the dependencies, the risks, the testing, the communications, the implementation plan and the rollback plan.
A change advisory board may advise on significant changes.
After the change is made, a post-implementation review checks the results and captures lessons for the future.
Finally, the tools.
Use version control, change tickets, configuration records, deployment logs, monitoring and automated pipelines to track changes.
These tools support accountability, but they do not replace judgment.
People must still decide whether a change is appropriate, safe and well understood.
